doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Future recording plans and selling his CDs
summary: He plans solo bass recordings and new songs with his son, and mentions selling his six CDs and being in the New York Swing trio.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well you’ve got a play in the future, a musical. Have you got any recording plans coming up soon?

Yes. Yes. I have a very ambitious project for myself. I am just getting into computerized recording now, and I’m going to create a whole series of recordings of just bass — solo bass songs of Ellington of this, that and the other thing, of different styles of music. I’m going to take also some classical themes and work on them, and see if I can play the classical themes and then find accompaniments to them, improvised accompaniments to them. And it’s songs that I really love from the classics, I mean as well as Gershwin and Porter and everybody else, and put out a long series of records, put them out myself, of bass solos on these things. Because bass solos are funny things. If they’re communicative, they find their way on to the air. Disc jockeys will play them.

The jazz guys will play a bass solo every once in a while, and they’ll just for the fun of it, stick it on. Then I’m going to do a whole lot of new songs of my own, with probably my son accompanying me mostly because he’s such a good keyboard player. And so I’ve got a lot of recording projects, just — big commercial plans in the recording world, no, I don’t see any reason for it. I don’t see what — I don’t understand how I could possibly © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

pull it off. But I’ll just keep doing my music and make it as good as I can, and I will try to sell it a bit more efficiently, through the Internet and stuff like that, and try to become a better salesman, as long as it doesn’t stress me out too much. Maybe I’ll just let other people —
It’s almost a whole job in itself to do that kind of thing. But you seem to have been very successful in finding a number of niches in the world of music.

Yes, I think so. I mean I’ve got record companies who still sell all six of my CDs now, I’m still talking to all the presidents of them, and the records are still on the market, and they still sell. And I’ve got deals coming up in the future, just some other stuff, and of course with Bucky and John — Bucky Pizzarelli and John Bunch, the group that got called New York Swing, that’s really a remarkable group to be in, I like this group very much, just piano, bass and guitar. And it’s a very interesting combination of older music, newer music, but all swinging and beautifully arranged, and these guys can play.
